title: CSS Flexbox
subtitle: Control Layouts With Confidence
description: Learn how to use CSS Flexbox to arrange, align, size, and distribute elements. You will build a responsive application interface while learning the reasoning behind every important Flexbox property.

blocks.text: Welcome to CSS Flexbox
You already know how CSS controls colors, spacing, borders, typography, and the box model.
Now we move into one of the most important layout systems you will use when building real interfaces.
That system is called Flexbox.
Flexbox helps you control how elements are arranged inside a container.
Open your editor and create a simple HTML page because we are going to build one interface throughout this lesson.
Your First Flex Container
Flexbox begins when you make an element a flex container.
The children inside that container then become flex items.
The property that activates Flexbox is display: flex.

blocks.text: Notice that gap belongs to the container because the container controls the spacing between its flex items.
The Main Axis and Cross Axis
Flexbox becomes much easier when you understand two directions: the main axis and the cross axis.
With the default row direction, the main axis runs horizontally and the cross axis runs vertically.
Many Flexbox properties make sense once you stop thinking in terms of left and right and start thinking in terms of these two axes.

blocks.title: See the Default Direction
blocks.output: Flex items are arranged horizontally.

blocks.title: Change the Main Axis
blocks.output: Flex items are now arranged vertically.

blocks.text: justify-content
justify-content controls how flex items are distributed along the main axis.
If your container uses the default row direction, justify-content controls horizontal distribution.

blocks.title: Center Items
blocks.output: The buttons move toward the center of the container.

blocks.title: Spread Items
blocks.output: The first item moves to the beginning, the last item moves to the end, and the remaining space is distributed between them.

blocks.text: Other useful values include flex-start, flex-end, space-around, and space-evenly.
align-items
align-items controls how flex items are positioned along the cross axis.
This property is one of the most useful tools for vertically aligning content.

blocks.title: Center Items Vertically
blocks.output: Items are centered along the cross axis.

blocks.title: Center a Complete Header
blocks.output: Header content is vertically aligned and distributed across the available width.

blocks.text: The Most Useful Centering Pattern
When you need to center an item horizontally and vertically inside a flex container, combine justify-content and align-items.

blocks.title: Perfect Centering
blocks.output: The content is centered in both directions.

blocks.text: This pattern appears everywhere in real interfaces, including cards, empty states, loading screens, buttons, and hero sections.
gap: The Clean Way to Space Items
You can use margins to create space between elements, but Flexbox gives you a cleaner container-level solution.

blocks.title: Use gap
blocks.output: Every flex item receives consistent spacing from its neighboring item.

blocks.text: The important idea is that gap describes the relationship between items rather than adding unnecessary spacing to the outside of individual elements.
flex-wrap
A row that fits on a large screen may become too wide on a phone.
flex-wrap allows items to move onto another line when there is not enough space.

blocks.title: Allow Wrapping
blocks.output: Items can move to another row instead of forcing horizontal overflow.

blocks.text: This is especially useful for tags, buttons, filters, navigation options, and responsive card layouts.
flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis
Flexbox can also control how individual items use available space.
flex-basis provides an initial size, flex-grow determines how an item can grow, and flex-shrink determines how it can shrink.

blocks.title: Flexible Columns
blocks.output: The sidebar keeps a 220px basis while the content takes the remaining available space.

blocks.text: The shorthand flex: 1 is extremely common when you want an item to take a fair share of remaining space.
align-self
Sometimes the container alignment is correct for most items but one item needs different alignment.

blocks.title: Override One Item
blocks.output: Only the selected flex item changes its cross-axis alignment.

blocks.text: order
The order property can visually rearrange flex items without changing the HTML order.

blocks.title: Change Visual Order
blocks.output: The featured item moves earlier in the visual Flexbox order.

blocks.text: Use this carefully because visual order and document order can affect how people navigate an interface.

blocks.text: Responsive Flexbox Thinking
Do not think of Flexbox as a collection of magic commands.
Think about what your container should do when the available space changes.
On a wide screen, several items may fit in one row.
On a narrow screen, wrapping or a changed direction may produce a better interface.

blocks.title: Mobile Layout
blocks.output: The header changes from a horizontal layout to a vertical layout.

blocks.text: Flexbox Debugging
When Flexbox does not behave as expected, inspect the container first.
Ask whether display: flex is applied to the correct parent.
Then identify the direction, main axis, cross axis, available width, gap, wrapping, and individual item sizing.

blocks.title: Debug the Container
blocks.output: This gives you a clear starting point for diagnosing a Flexbox layout.

blocks.text: Your Flexbox Challenge
Build a dashboard header containing a logo, navigation links, and a user button.
Use Flexbox to keep the main elements aligned and use gap for consistent spacing.
Create a course section containing at least three cards.
Make the cards wrap when the available width becomes too small.
Finally, create a mobile layout where the header content stacks vertically.
Critical Flexbox Assessment

blocks.question: You want the children of .menu to become Flexbox items. Which declaration must be applied to .menu?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. display: flex turns the element into a flex container, making its direct children flex items.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Flexbox begins by turning the parent into a flex container.
blocks.reasoning: Flexbox is applied to the parent. Once display: flex is used, its direct children participate in the Flexbox layout.

blocks.question: A flex container uses flex-direction: row. You want the items centered horizontally. Which property is the most direct choice?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. With row direction, the main axis is horizontal, so justify-content controls horizontal distribution.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the main axis. With row direction, horizontal positioning is controlled by justify-content.
blocks.reasoning: justify-content controls the main axis. Because row creates a horizontal main axis, justify-content: center centers the items horizontally.
blocks.hint: Row means the main axis runs horizontally.

blocks.question: You want a row of buttons to move onto another line when the screen becomes too narrow. Which declaration is most appropriate?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. flex-wrap: wrap allows flex items to move onto additional lines when necessary.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The property that controls whether flex items can create additional lines is flex-wrap.
blocks.reasoning: Without wrapping, a row may remain on one line and create cramped content or overflow. flex-wrap: wrap allows the layout to adapt.
blocks.hint: Look for the Flexbox property containing the word wrap.

blocks.question: A header has a logo on the left and a profile button on the right. Which combination most directly creates this layout?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Flexbox with justify-content: space-between pushes the first item toward one end and the last item toward the other.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: You need a Flexbox container plus main-axis distribution that separates the first and last items.
blocks.reasoning: With the default row direction, justify-content: space-between distributes the remaining horizontal space between the flex items.
blocks.hint: Think about distributing extra space between the first and last items.

blocks.question: You need one Flexbox child to take most of the remaining available width while another child stays at a fixed basis. Which pattern is most appropriate?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. flex: 1 allows the content area to use remaining space while flex: 0 0 220px gives the sidebar a fixed basis.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Focus on which item should absorb the remaining space and which item should maintain a fixed basis.
blocks.reasoning: flex: 1 is a common way to make one item flexible. The 0 0 220px shorthand prevents the sidebar from growing or shrinking and gives it a 220px basis.
blocks.hint: Which item should consume leftover space?

blocks.question: A Flexbox container uses flex-direction: column. You want its children centered horizontally. Which property should you normally use?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. With column direction, the main axis becomes vertical, so the horizontal direction is the cross axis controlled by align-items.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The direction changed. With column, horizontal positioning is now the cross axis.
blocks.reasoning: Flexbox properties depend on the axes. In column mode, align-items controls the horizontal cross axis.
blocks.hint: Column changes the main axis from horizontal to vertical.

blocks.question: Three course cards look fine on desktop but force horizontal overflow on a small phone. Which Flexbox improvement is the best first step?
options: Use flex-wrap: wrap with an appropriate flexible basis.
Use position: absolute on every card.
Increase the fixed width of every card.
Set overflow-x: hidden and ignore the layout.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Wrapping with a sensible flexible basis lets the cards adapt instead of forcing them into one row.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Hiding overflow does not solve the underlying layout problem. Make the layout capable of adapting.
blocks.reasoning: Responsive design should allow content to reflow. flex-wrap combined with flexible sizing gives the cards a way to move onto additional lines.
blocks.hint: Solve the layout rather than hiding its overflow.

blocks.question: You have five navigation links and want equal 16px spacing between them. Which approach is the cleanest container-level solution?
options: Add margin-left: 16px to every link, including the first.
Set gap: 16px on the flex container.
Set padding: 16px on the flex container.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. gap is designed to control spacing between flex items without creating unnecessary outside spacing.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the Flexbox property specifically designed to create consistent space between items.
blocks.reasoning: gap expresses the relationship between neighboring flex items. It is cleaner than manually adding margins to individual children.
blocks.hint: Which property literally describes space between layout items?

blocks.question: A dashboard has a sidebar and main content area. The sidebar should stay around 220px while the content uses the remaining width. Which design best matches that requirement?
options: Sidebar uses flex: 0 0 220px; and content uses flex: 1;
Sidebar uses flex: 1; and content uses width: 220px;
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The sidebar receives a fixed 220px flex basis while the content absorbs remaining space.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: One element needs a controlled basis while the other needs to remain flexible.
blocks.reasoning: The sidebar is defined as 220px with flex: 0 0 220px. The content's flex: 1 tells it to use the remaining available space.
blocks.hint: Which element has the fixed requirement?

blocks.text: What You Should Understand Before Moving On
You should now be able to identify the Flexbox container and its direct children.
You should understand the difference between the main axis and cross axis.
You should know when to use flex-direction, justify-content, align-items, gap, flex-wrap, and flexible sizing.
Most importantly, you should be able to look at a layout problem and choose the Flexbox property that solves the actual problem instead of randomly changing CSS.
This is the skill that will matter when you begin combining Flexbox with Grid and responsive design in the next lessons.
Lesson 6 Complete
You have learned how to build flexible one-dimensional layouts with CSS Flexbox.
HTML gives your application structure, CSS gives it visual design, and Flexbox gives you powerful control over how interface elements are arranged.
In the next lesson, you will learn CSS Grid and how it can control more complex two-dimensional layouts.
